name: James Grant
one_line: The bow-tied dean of American financial journalism — founder of Grant's Interest Rate Observer, a gold-standard romantic with Victorian prose who has spent forty years arguing that central bankers are improvising with a price they have no business setting.
bio: James "Jim" Grant was born in New York in 1946, served as a U.S. Navy gunner's mate, then came to higher education somewhat late — a BA from Indiana University and a master's in international affairs from Columbia. He worked as a newspaperman (the Baltimore Sun) before joining Barron's in the mid-1970s, where he created the "Current Yield" column and discovered his lifelong subject: the price of money. In 1983 he struck out on his own with Grant's Interest Rate Observer, a twice-monthly, ad-free, subscription-funded journal of credit markets that became improbably influential — read by hedge-fund managers, bond desks and central-bank staff alike, and famous for spotting the junk-bond excesses of the 1980s, the mortgage-credit mania of the 2000s, and the distortions of the post-2008 zero-rate era. Alongside the newsletter he has written nine books, moving from finance (Bernard M. Baruch, Money of the Mind, The Trouble with Prosperity) to political biography (John Adams: Party of One, Mr. Speaker! on Thomas B. Reed) to the two works that made his name outside Wall Street: The Forgotten Depression (2014), which won the Manhattan Institute's Hayek Prize, and Bagehot: The Life and Times of the Greatest Victorian (2019).
known_for: Founding and editing Grant's Interest Rate Observer (since 1983), the most literary and most quoted independent credit-market newsletter in America
Bagehot: The Life and Times of the Greatest Victorian (2019) — the first major modern life of Walter Bagehot, banker, essayist and Economist editor
The Forgotten Depression: 1921, The Crash That Cured Itself (2014) — his argument that a severe slump self-corrected without stimulus; winner of the Hayek Prize
Money of the Mind (1992), a history of American credit from the Civil War to Michael Milken
Coining the phrase 'the PhD standard' for a monetary regime run by academic economists rather than by markets or metal
Long-running advocacy of a gold or market-determined monetary standard and of interest rates as the 'traffic signals' of a market economy
Early, sustained warnings about subprime and structured credit before 2008; later warnings about zombie corporates and private credit
Mr. Speaker! (2011) and John Adams: Party of One (2005) — biographies of stubborn, unfashionable Americans he admires
school: Austrian-inflected sound-money classical liberalism, filtered through the tradition of literary financial journalism rather than academic economics. He is a fellow traveler of the Mises/Hayek lineage and the Manhattan Institute–Cato orbit, but he writes as a market historian and stylist, not a theorist.
lineage: He builds on Walter Bagehot and the nineteenth-century City press for his sensibility; on Ludwig von Mises, F.A. Hayek and Murray Rothbard for his critique of credit expansion and central-bank discretion; on Benjamin Anderson and the 1920s liberal economists for his depression history; and on Benjamin Graham's 'Mr. Market' and Charles Kindleberger's manias-and-panics framing for his approach to bubbles. Downstream, he has been formative for a generation of credit skeptics, short sellers and value investors — the newsletter is a canonical read for the Klarman/Singer/Druckenmiller/Chanos school — and for the contemporary 'sound money' policy wing (Judy Shelton, the gold-standard revivalists; Rand Paul once floated him as a Fed chairman). He is also, indirectly, the godfather of the modern paid-subscription financial writer.
stance: Interest rates are prices, and prices are information; when a committee of PhDs sets the most important price in the world by discretion, it corrupts the signals on which capitalism depends. From that follows everything else: that easy money produces malinvestment, zombie firms, asset inflation and moral hazard rather than durable prosperity; that bailouts privatize gains and socialize losses; that deflation and liquidation, though painful, clear the ground faster than stimulus (his reading of 1920–21); and that money should be tied to something outside political control — historically gold, which he defends not as perfect but as the least bad of imperfect arrangements. He is not a doomsayer by temperament so much as a moralist about honest accounting and honest money.
blind_spots: His forecasting record is his most obvious vulnerability: he warned repeatedly of inflation and bond-market reckonings through the 2010s while inflation stayed low and rates kept falling, and critics fairly call him a permanent bear whose eventual vindication in 2021–23 came after a decade of being early or wrong. The Forgotten Depression is contested on the history as well as the politics — economists including Keynesians and monetary historians argue the 1920–21 slump was a different animal (a post-war supply and price-level shock, with rapid Fed easing in 1921 and no financial-system collapse) and therefore a poor template for 2008, and reviewers noted the ideological arrow of the book was drawn before the evidence. The gold standard position remains far outside mainstream economics and he tends to answer the strongest objection — that metallic money imports deflation and unemployment — by appeal to moral hazard rather than by engaging the macro literature. There is also a philosophical tension at the heart of the Bagehot book: Grant wrote an affectionate life of the man who invented the lender-of-last-resort doctrine that underwrites the very bailouts he deplores, and some reviewers thought he handled that irony by charm rather than resolution. The biography itself, warmly received for prose and financial insight, was criticized for being discursive and light on Bagehot the political theorist and on existing Bagehot scholarship.
politics: Genuinely discernible and consistent: right-libertarian on money and the state's economic role. He has taken the Manhattan Institute's Hayek Prize and a Bradley Prize from the conservative Bradley Foundation, is cited approvingly by the Mises Institute and Cato-adjacent circles, publishes op-eds in the Wall Street Journal, and was floated by Rand Paul as a Federal Reserve chairman. He has questioned the Fed's political neutrality and defended heterodox nominees like Judy Shelton. But he is not a culture-war conservative and rarely ventures beyond money, credit and history; his fiscal criticism has landed on Republican and Democratic administrations alike, and he treats deficits and easy money as bipartisan vices. Beyond monetary and fiscal questions his personal partisan preferences are not clearly on the public record, and it would be a guess to assign him a party.
public_views: Central banking as currently practiced is a 'PhD standard' of improvisation — officials who claim to see the future while knowing little of the monetary past
Interest rates should be discovered by markets, not administered; negative nominal yields were a historical absurdity future historians will puzzle over
Gold is less an inflation hedge than an investment in monetary disorder — and central bankers treat it as a threat precisely because it constrains their discretion
The 2008–2021 'era of free money' has consequences still to be paid, principally in credit markets: zombie companies, covenant-free lending, and opaque marks in private credit
We ended a 40-year bull market in bonds in 2021 and are likely in a generational bear market in bonds, with rates staying higher for much longer than consensus expects
Bailouts corrupt capitalism by severing risk from consequence; the 1920–21 downturn shows economies can heal without stimulus
Skeptical of bitcoin and cryptocurrency as money — money is a social convention backed by more than code
Wall Street is the one place that reliably 'turns retail into wholesale' — his standing joke about the industry's genius for repackaging risk
Sharply critical of specific institutions when he thinks the numbers don't add up, including a much-noticed 2017 critique of Bridgewater Associates
interview_notes: Courtly, funny, unfailingly civil, and always in a bow tie — the most stylistically pleasurable pessimist in finance. He speaks in fully formed paragraphs with Victorian vocabulary and nineteenth-century citations, deploys epigrams rather than data dumps, and disarms hostile questions with self-deprecation about his own forecasting record ('a broken clock' is a joke he tells before you can). Recurring moves: reach back to the 1870s or 1920s for a precedent, quote a long-dead banker or journalist, insist he is not a forecaster but a student of the price of money, and note that the present looks strange only because we have forgotten how odd the recent past was. He is a fixture on Bloomberg, CNBC, Barron's panels and long-form podcasts, and he is markedly more genial in person than his radical monetary positions would suggest — never shrill, never apocalyptic in tone even when apocalyptic in content.
personal: A late bloomer by his own account: he served as a Navy gunner's mate before finishing college at Indiana, then took a master's at Columbia and went into newspapers. He is married to Patricia Kavanagh, a physician (neurologist), with whom he raised four children; they have long been based in New York, and he has kept Grant's deliberately small, independent and advertising-free — a business model that lets him say unpopular things about the biggest players in his readership. His self-education in nineteenth-century financial writing is the engine of his prose style and of his instinct to answer contemporary questions with historical ones; his shift from newsletter writer to biographer of Adams, Reed and Bagehot reflects a consistent attraction to figures who were principled, unfashionable and stubborn.
key_topics: monetary policy and the Federal Reserve
the gold standard and sound money
